name: Lower facelift with neck lift

lead: A lower facelift with neck lift targets jowls, the jawline and the neck together. It typically tightens deeper layers (the SMAS), may tighten the platysma muscle band of the neck, removes or contours fat under the chin, and trims and redrapes skin.

Published reports are mostly from surgeons describing their combined techniques, including one team that argues combinations of methods are essential for lasting results. Registered trials include comparisons of office-based limited and hospital-based full facelifts.

paras: Facelift tightening of SMAS or deep-plane tissue lifts the jowls, while platysma work, submental lipectomy and sometimes chin implants reshape the neck and under-chin contour.

Facelift complications documented include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss; smoking raises the risk. Wikipedia notes the greater auricular nerve is the most frequently injured sensory nerve.

lead: A lower facelift with neck lift is a combined surgical approach to the jowls, jawline and neck, in which facelift tightening of the SMAS or deeper tissues is performed together with treatment of neck structures such as the platysma muscle and submental fat.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that a traditional facelift addresses neck skin and platysma laxity.[1]

A 1983 anatomical and clinical report from nearly 100 patients described anterior neck principles combining submandibular lipectomy, excision of the submental fat pad, chin implantation, creation or tightening of a platysma muscular sling, and skin tightening or resection.[3] A 2018 team's lower face and neck rejuvenation combined method uses liposuction, lipectomy, myotomies, suspensions and tissue-induction techniques, arguing that combinations are essential for satisfactory lasting results.[2]

Other surgeons report SMAS plication with periauricular purse-string and malar fat pad elevation evaluated with FACE-Q,[4] and endoscopic deep plane facelifts with a classification for patient selection.[5] Evidence is mostly case series.
infobox: SMAS tightening, platysma work, submental fat removal[3]

paras: Neck aging involves platysma laxity and submental fat. Surgeons treat it by approximating or tightening the platysma, removing fat and sometimes adding a chin implant, in addition to skin redraping.[3] Deep plane facelifts dissect beneath the SMAS so that skin and deeper tissue move together and ligaments are released.[1][6]

Reported variants include the combined lower face and neck method,[2] SMAS plication with purse-string and malar fat pad elevation,[4] and endoscopic deep plane approaches described in 2025 as offering scar-concealed access.[5] Wikipedia describes skin-only, SMAS, deep-plane and composite variants.[1]

Wikipedia lists hematoma as the most common facelift complication, with nerve injury (greater auricular sensory; facial motor), skin necrosis (smoking raises risk about twelvefold), scarring, hair loss, ear changes and a windswept look if skin is over-removed or the vector insufficiently vertical.[1]

Published studies are surgeon-reported. The 2018 combined method paper describes outcomes of its approach,[2] and a 2018 paper reports patient-reported FACE-Q outcomes for a plication technique.[4] A 2025 paper presents a classification for endoscopic deep plane facelift.[5] Registered trials include a 100-patient comparison of an office-based limited facelift with a hospital-based full facelift (status unknown),[7] a small histology study of a skin treatment as adjunct to facelift surgery (n=7, completed),[8] and a phase 2/3 trial of tacrolimus for malar edema.[9] No published results from these registrations were found.

timeline.event: Anterior neck and platysma principles reported from nearly 100 patients.[3]
